rv.q: If you’ve ever seen the fantastic Groff in concert, you know he’s a singer who loves to make eye contact with audience members. That quality — his desire for personal connection — is what makes him such a strong, layered, sympathetic Frank. And his hopeful glance is what sells an unobtrusive but vital new ending.

Broadway never saw a better triple-act than Jonathan Groff, Lindsay Mendez and Daniel Radcliffe, the triumphant triumvirate at the heart of the gorgeous new revival of “Merrily Along” directed by the famed British musical theater star Maria Friedman.
On a larger stage, it shines as an even more luminous achievement.

Director Maria Friedman, in league with stars Jonathan Groff, Lindsay Mendez and Daniel Radcliffe, burrow down to the musical’s theatrical core and discover not a shallow pool of glibness but a deep wellspring of emotionality.

Friedman’s production meets the audience halfway, and a Broadway audience today just might be able to make up the difference as it couldn’t in 1981. Cross your fingers: It might finally be ’Merrily’s’ time.
Friedman and her ensemble render the show exquisite.
It's no small wonder that this sensational revival manages to synthesize the famous flop's unwieldy ambitions into a palpable hit.
Groff, always a compelling actor, here steps up to an unmissable one.
You’d be hard-pressed to imagine a better Merrily Along.
It’s the greatest thing in the show.

More indelible than the pleasures of its performances or score, more incisive than its familiar assurance that being a rich Hollywood producer is, in fact, the worst, is 'Merrily's' willingness to take a complicated view of friendship.
Because of the cultural shift that happened between the time Sondheim wrote the musical and now, both Charly and Mary's disappointment in Frank can seem petty and codependent.

Radcliffe is very competent in the role — he's believable as a driven playwright committed to the purity of his art, and he's fun, with moments of brilliance — but he doesn't have the kind of stage presence of seasoned Broadway actors Groff and Mendez.
All told, it’s a hit, to borrow a title phrase from one of Sondheim most artful “concerted” numbers; a palpable hit, to borrow a phrase the Master borrowed from the Bard.
Thankfully, Friedman has found three actors whose charm and genuine connection overrides their characters’ most unpalatable qualities.
“Merrily” is the most top-to-bottom perfect production of them all, from its muscular orchestrations to its vibrant ensemble to its sneakily devastating book by the late George Furth.
So don't let another day go by without grabbing tickets to this must-see production!
Sitting comfortably in the Hudson Theatre, this Merrily is one of those transcendent productions I’ll look back on fondly forever.
Some true theatre magic is happening on that stage, and for that we will forever be grateful.
Better yet, I recommend getting a ticket to see this wonderful “Merrily” revival and buy another the following week to enjoy it even more the second time.
You’re going to want to preserve the riches flowing throughout this hurts-so-good musical about growing up and growing apart.
The lyrics and music are Sondheim at his most waspish and wise; days later, the songs are still buzzing in my mind, insisting on being hummed.
Well, more than four decades after it premiered to quizzical expressions, Merrily Along is a hit.
Friedman and her star-studded cast have succeeded in wrangling Merrily into a powerful hit filled with big laughs and equally big heartbreaks.
Director Maria Friedman doesn’t eliminate what’s off-putting about “Merrily Along”; instead she directs our attention to what’s best about it.
Moment for moment, it is the most intensely emotional show on a Broadway stage in recent memory.
It showcases skillful acting and singing by the original cast and puts Sondheim’s imagination, playfulness, and mastery of composition and lyric writing on glorious display.
And yet, not one second in this musical registers as a cynical exercise.
It’s messy, ambitious, and deeply layered in a way that really sticks long after the credits roll.
I felt like director Maria Friedman made the most out of this musical that was possible within the constraints of what is written on the page.

cn.t: Critics hail this triumphant revival as finally cracking the code of Sondheim's 1981 flop. The stellar trio of Groff, Radcliffe, and Mendez deliver heartbreaking performances in a production that's as close to perfect as Broadway gets.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored 1903 gem — one of the most gorgeous small theaters on Broadway. The 2017 renovation delivered some of the widest and most comfortable seats in the Theater District, with excellent sightlines from the intimate 970-seat house.
